svg.title: P029 · Order value and units by shipper
svg.desc: Work through the three-order example from its original rows to shipper totals. Blue comes from Orders, green from Shippers and red from OrderDetails. The CTE and two left joins keep order 10’s amount of 100 once. A separate check shows order 16 retaining 80 while its final units total becomes zero.
svg.text: Order value and units by shipper
Follow order 10 from its two detail lines to FastShip’s single report row.
A dark band names the source above each set of columns. ƒ marks a calculated value. A pointer marks the row to follow. Double underlines mark

g.text: One order can have several detail lines. Sum the quantities for each OrderID so the summary can match an order at most once.
Order 10 contributes 2 + 3 = 5 units. The other orders contribute 4 and 1. All 10 units are accounted for.

g.aria-label: Why start the outer query with Orders?
g.text: 2. Why start the outer query with Orders?
The report counts orders and adds their amounts. Orders supplies one row per order and both IDs needed for the later lookups.

g.aria-label: Report starts with these three orders
g.data-table: Report starts with these three orders
g.text: Report starts with these three orders
Order 10 enters with its amount of 100 on a single row. An order can enter even when its shipper or its detail rows are missing.

g.aria-label: Why add Shippers with a LEFT JOIN?
g.text: 3. Why add Shippers with a LEFT JOIN?
Orders already carries ShipperID. Add Shippers second to look up its company name. Every order stays on the left, including an
order with an unrecognised shipper ID.
Orders 10 and 11 both find FastShip. A missing lookup would leave the green columns NULL. A shipper with no orders supplies no report

g.aria-label: Separate check · two missing shipper matches
g.text: Separate check · two different orders with no matching shipper
Add order 15 with shipper ID 99 and order 17 with a missing ID. Their amounts are 40 and 30. Both orders survive the first join.

g.aria-label: Rows from the first LEFT JOIN
g.data-table: Rows from the first LEFT JOIN
g.text: Rows from the first LEFT JOIN
Both names become Unknown shipper. With 3 and 2 units respectively, these orders form one group worth 70 with 5 units.

g.aria-label: Why LEFT JOIN the units summary third?
g.text: 4. Why LEFT JOIN the units summary third?
The previous result still carries Orders.OrderID. Attach the prepared units total on that key. A left join keeps the order amount even
if the summary has no row.
Order 10 now carries amount 100 and 5 units. Both joins match directly to Orders, so these two lookups can trade places once the units
Separate check · OtherShip has one order and no detail lines
Add shipper 3, OtherShip, and order 16 worth 80. These extra rows belong only to this check.
SUM has no known units to add here. The outer COALESCE supplies 0 while the order still contributes 80 in value.

g.aria-label: Why use the displayed shipper name for grouping?
g.text: 5. Why use the displayed shipper name for grouping?
Each order contributes to one reporting label. COALESCE gives an unmatched lookup the label Unknown shipper so missing and
unrecognised IDs feed the same group.
FastShip receives orders 10 and 11. SlowShip receives order 12. All three order IDs occur exactly once before the shipper totals are

g.aria-label: Why count, add and then sort?
g.text: 6. Why count, add and then sort?
Count the order IDs, add each order amount once and add its units total. COALESCE turns a group’s all-NULL units total into zero.
Sort the shipper totals by order value, highest first.

g.aria-label: How each shipper total is calculated
g.data-table: How each shipper total is calculated
g.text: How each shipper total is calculated
FastShip comes first because 300 exceeds 50. The two rows account for all 3 orders, 350 in order value and 10 units.
